75 Varick St, 5th Floor 
New York, NY 10013 
 
June 15, 2026 
 
Dr. Mehmet Oz 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
Attn: CMS–0042–NC 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244-8013 
 
Submitted electronically via: http://www.regulations.gov 
 
RE: File Code CMS-0062-P - Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care 
Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, 
Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) 
Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the 
Federally-Facilitated Exchanges 
   
Dear Administrator Oz, 
 
Oscar Health, Inc. (“Oscar”) is a healthcare technology company committed to leveraging data-driven 
solutions to help our members live healthier lives. We envision a healthcare system in which technology, 
including responsibly deployed artificial intelligence (AI), reduces friction for patients, providers, and 
issuers, and streamlines challenging administrative processes such as prior authorization. By aligning 
stakeholders to standardized Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)-based application 
programming interfaces (APIs), the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) will improve 
patient engagement, enhance care delivery, and reduce administrative burdens. CMS has already made 
meaningful progress advancing interoperability, including through the launch of the Digital Health 
Ecosystem,1 which Oscar joined to support the modernization of healthcare infrastructure. Oscar 
welcomes the expansion of these rules to drugs in the CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior 
Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule (“Proposed Rule”). 
 
To deliver on CMS’s commitment to create a more streamlined, transparent, and reliable prior 
authorization process, we recommend that CMS take the following steps: 
 
1.​ Incentivize shared accountability for modernizing the prior authorization process; 
2.​ Optimize real-time data exchange by reducing administrative burdens; and  
3.​ Promote sandbox testing that balances oversight and innovation. 
 
1.​ Incentivize shared accountability for modernizing the prior authorization process. 
 
A streamlined, consumer-centric prior authorization process depends on meaningful collaboration and 
transparent, comprehensive information sharing between issuers and providers. The Provider Access, 
Patient Access, Payer-to-Payer, and Prior Authorization APIs are important steps toward a more 
connected healthcare system, but they can only achieve their full potential if accurate, complete clinical 
1 Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. (n.d.). Health technology ecosystem. 
https://www.cms.gov/priorities/health-technology-ecosystem/overview 
1 
 
information enters the system at the point of care. Without provider participation, gaps in clinical data will 
follow patients across providers, issuers, and care settings, limiting the ability of interoperability tools to 
empower patients and support seamless care. Issuers frequently receive flawed data, ranging from 
incomplete clinical histories to information belonging to the wrong patient. An estimated 28% to 35% of 
all prior authorization denials can be attributed to missing or inaccurate information2 exacerbated by 
pervasive manual workflows. A 2022 American Medical Association survey, for example, found that 59% 
of physicians surveyed completed prior authorizations by phone, while 45% still used fax machines.3 
Continued reliance on fax, phone, or other manual channels risks undermining the efficiencies the 
electronic prior authorization (ePA) infrastructure is intended to deliver. 
 
To optimize prior authorization, CMS should incentivize providers to share accountability for 
modernizing workflows and data-sharing practices. Specifically, CMS should require providers that 
accept Medicare and Medicaid patients to submit requests electronically, accompanied by the 
complete clinical data necessary for a full review. As a large number of providers that serve Medicaid 
or Medicare beneficiaries also accept commercial insurance, this requirement would likely accelerate 
timely, accurate, and structured clinical data submission for the entire industry. With better data, issuers 
could improve the prior authorization process by: 
 
●​ Deploying responsible AI and automation for approvals. Responsibly deployed AI and 
automation would help accelerate approvals, reducing administrative burden and improving the 
patient experience. As part of recent industry prior authorization commitments, Oscar and other 
issuers have committed to approving at least 80% of medical ePA requests in real-time.4 
Requiring or incentivizing providers to submit prior authorizations electronically would enable 
issuers to make additional progress.  
 
●​ Identifying potential FWA through complete clinical data. Complete clinical data would help 
issuers identify potential fraud, waste, and abuse (FWA) by documenting prior surgeries, 
procedures, and medications across previous issuers. This would enable new issuers to quickly 
advance a patient’s treatment plan rather than duplicating treatments or medications already 
received, reducing administrative costs, provider burden, and patient confusion during issuer 
transitions. Over time, issuers could also use this data to strengthen FWA prevention efforts  
including by building automated mechanisms to compare clinical codes to a patient’s clinical 
record. 
 
●​ Advancing continuity of care through robust clinical data. As part of industry’s prior 
authorization commitments for medical services, Oscar and other issuers have committed to 
honoring existing prior authorizations for benefit-equivalent in-network services as part of a 
90-day transition period.5 Robust clinical data would further allow issuers to build a more 
comprehensive clinical history for patients, promoting increased continuity of care and allowing 
issuers to conduct tailored outreach to inform members of personalized programs or plans, such 
as Oscar’s Diabetes program.6 Additionally, comprehensive data would increase accuracy and 
reduce administrative burden for External Data Gathering Environment (EDGE) claim 
submissions.    
 
6Oscar Health. (n.d.). Meet the plan designed to support diabetes care. https://www.hioscar.com/diabetes 
5AHIP. (2025, June). Improving prior authorization for patients & providers. 
4AHIP. (2025, June). Improving prior authorization for patients & providers. 
3American Medical Association. (2022, October). Why the end could be near for prior-authorization faxes. 
2Muni Health. (2026, May). Prior authorization denied? Complete 2026 action guide for providers. 
2 
 
2.​ Optimize real-time data exchange by reducing administrative burdens. 
 
The Proposed Rule offers an opportunity to expand existing APIs to streamline prior authorization and 
give patients a more complete medical history that includes prescription drugs. To amplify innovation, 
CMS should develop resources that ease administrative burdens on developers. We offer the following 
technical recommendations: 
 
●​ Establish a central repository for API endpoints. CMS should develop a centralized repository 
for issuers to report API endpoints for each required interoperability API. This centralized 
directory would reduce the administrative burden on both issuers and the agency by eliminating 
the need to search for individual endpoints. Furthermore, collecting API endpoints alone should 
obviate the need for CMS to collect a direct URL for FHIR capability statements. Oscar also 
supports CMS requiring issuers to provide a single URL to a site that contains authorization and 
authentication protocols and implementation details. 
 
●​ Align reporting requirements with the NDH IG Resource. We support aligning reporting 
requirements with the National Directory of Healthcare Providers & Services (NDH) 
Implementation Guide (IG) Endpoint Profile resource, which would streamline updates and 
prevent redundancies by replacing manual updates with a single FHIR resource. Though there 
would be development costs, this alignment would likely reduce issuer burden to manually report 
in the long-term. If CMS finalizes the NDH IG as an alternative proposal, we request an 
implementation deadline of 90 days after the final rule’s effective date. This would ensure issuers 
have adequate time to adjust and prepare for any significant upfront operational updates.  
 
●​ Limit the number of mandatory IGs. Oscar supports mandatory implementation guides (IGs) 
because true interoperability depends on standardization. However, to ensure smooth transitions, 
CMS should provide a predictable lifecycle that avoids the burden of maintaining multiple 
unexpired IG versions at once. We recommend that CMS establish guardrails to either set 
timelines for issuers to retire older IG versions or minimize the total number of IGs issuers must 
support simultaneously. This would help reduce the operational burden on issuers—especially 
those developing native technologies.  
 
3.​ Promote sandbox testing that balances oversight and innovation. 
 
To ensure robust interoperability without introducing production instability, CMS should formalize the 
use of public sandbox environments populated with synthetic datasets. A sandbox allows CMS or 
accredited testing bodies to run automated validation suites to verify structural conformance before 
deployment. For providers and third-party developers, sandboxes also provide a reliable environment to 
test endpoints and validate implementation with the payer’s API before production use. 
 
In response to the Request for Input (RFI) Questions regarding Roadmap for Consistent Implementation 
of Payer API Technology and Certification of Payer API Technology, we recommend: 
 
●​ Evaluate testing tools through core criteria. CMS should evaluate testing tools based on three 
core criteria: (1) IG profile validation support; (2) sandbox compatibility, meaning the tool is 
natively designed to run against synthetic data environments; and (3) public availability and 
accessibility. 
 
●​ Refrain from mandating rigid testing requirements. CMS should not mandate interoperability 
testing beyond initial conformance validation. Multi-system testing varies significantly across 
3 
 
issuers, making it less suitable for rigid regulatory standards. Structural conformance to required 
IGs paired with a public sandbox provides client applications with the framework to achieve 
successful integration. 
 
●​ Standardize test suites. As an intermediate step toward formal API certification, CMS should 
focus on publishing standardized conformance test suites that issuers can run against their own 
sandbox environments. This phased approach would allow issuers to self-validate during 
development while giving CMS real-time visibility into industry readiness. Once these 
standardized tools mature and issuers have stabilized their implementations, CMS can evaluate 
the necessity of a formal certification program based on real-world data. 
 
Implications for ICHRA 
 
Finally, while the Proposed Rule makes significant progress for consumers transitioning between issuers 
within the individual market, its impact remains limited for those utilizing Individual Coverage Health 
Reimbursement Arrangements (ICHRAs). For example, if a consumer is new to an ICHRA and is 
transitioning from a large-group plan into an individual-market plan, the former issuer would not be 
required to send the patient’s data to the new issuer, potentially resulting in gaps in the patient's medical 
history. We urge CMS to explore more ways to incentivize interoperability across all healthcare markets 
(e.g., individual, Medicaid, large group, Medicare) to ensure patients can easily access complete medical 
records over the course of their life. 
 
Conclusion 
 
Oscar appreciates the opportunity to weigh in on these proposed interoperability standards. We believe 
that simplifying prior authorization requires clear, scalable technical boundaries that protect innovation 
while eliminating administrative friction. We thank CMS for its consideration of these recommendations, 
and we look forward to partnering with the agency to achieve our shared goals. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Cathy Grason  
Vice President and Head of Government Affairs

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Oscar Health, Inc.; signed by Cathy Grason, Vice President and Head of Government Affairs.
- **Stakeholder type:** Payer / Technology-enabled health insurer.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Oscar describes itself as a healthcare technology company using data-driven solutions and responsibly deployed AI. It notes participation in CMS's Digital Health Ecosystem.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Oscar supports expanding interoperability and prior authorization requirements to drugs and emphasizes shared accountability, real-time data exchange, and testing infrastructure. It recommends requiring or incentivizing providers to submit electronic PA requests with complete clinical data, creating a centralized API endpoint repository, aligning endpoint reporting with the NDH IG Endpoint Profile, limiting simultaneous mandatory IG version burden, using public sandboxes with synthetic data, and improving interoperability across markets including ICHRAs.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS/RFI certification issues; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P; no CFR sections cited.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR-based APIs; Provider Access API; Patient Access API; Payer-to-Payer API; Prior Authorization API; NDH IG Endpoint Profile resource; implementation guides; sandbox conformance testing.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Shared accountability for electronic PA**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Oscar argues payer APIs can only work if complete, accurate clinical data enter the system at the point of care. It cites missing or inaccurate information as a major cause of denials and manual workflows as a barrier.
- **Specific request:** Require providers accepting Medicare and Medicaid patients to submit PA requests electronically with complete clinical data needed for review.

**Topic 2: Responsible AI and automation enabled by complete data**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Complete structured data could support real-time approvals, FWA detection, continuity of care, and reduced duplication during issuer transitions.
- **Specific request:** Encourage electronic clinical data submission to allow responsible AI/automation and better continuity workflows.

**Topic 3: Centralized API endpoint repository**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** A centralized repository would reduce issuer, CMS, developer, and provider burden by eliminating payer-by-payer endpoint searching.
- **Specific request:** CMS should develop a centralized repository for all required interoperability API endpoints; endpoint collection alone should eliminate the need to collect a direct FHIR capability-statement URL; issuers should provide a single URL for authorization/authentication protocols and implementation details.

**Topic 4: NDH IG Endpoint Profile alignment**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Using the NDH IG Endpoint Profile would streamline updates and reduce manual reporting redundancy.
- **Specific request:** Align reporting requirements with the NDH IG Endpoint Profile resource and allow 90 days after final rule effective date if finalized as an alternative.

**Topic 5: Limit mandatory IG version burden**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Oscar supports mandatory IGs for interoperability but warns against requiring simultaneous maintenance of too many unexpired versions.
- **Specific request:** Establish guardrails to set retirement timelines for older IG versions or minimize the number of IGs issuers must support at once.

**Topic 6: Sandbox testing and certification roadmap**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS implementation/certification issues
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Public sandboxes with synthetic data can verify structural conformance without production instability and give providers/developers reliable test environments.
- **Specific request:** Formalize public sandbox environments; evaluate testing tools based on IG profile validation, sandbox compatibility, and public availability; publish standardized conformance test suites; avoid rigid multi-system testing beyond initial conformance validation.

**Topic 7: ICHRA and cross-market interoperability gaps**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Clarify / Modify
- **Rationale:** ICHRA users moving from large-group to individual-market coverage may not receive full payer-to-payer data exchange, causing medical history gaps.
- **Specific request:** Explore incentives for interoperability across individual, Medicaid, large group, and Medicare markets.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1:** Oscar supports mandatory IGs because standardization is necessary for true interoperability.
- **S2/S3:** Oscar requests predictable IG lifecycle guardrails, retirement timelines for older versions, and limits on simultaneous IG support.
- **S23/S24/S26/S27/S33:** Oscar supports a centralized API endpoint repository, a single implementation/authentication URL, and NDH IG Endpoint Profile alignment.
- **S29/S34/S35:** Oscar addresses API reporting burden indirectly through endpoint reporting and standardized resources rather than detailed usage metric design.
- **S37:** Oscar identifies operational burdens of multiple IGs and developer implementation complexity.
- **S54:** Oscar recommends public sandboxes, synthetic datasets, automated validation suites, and standardized conformance test suites as a pathway toward certification.
- **S66-S82:** Oscar responds to payer API technology/certification RFI issues and cross-market interoperability issues, including ICHRAs.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Incentivize or require providers accepting Medicare and Medicaid patients to submit PA requests electronically with complete clinical data.
2. Use complete structured data to support responsible AI, automation, FWA detection, and continuity of care.
3. Create a centralized CMS repository for API endpoints for each required interoperability API.
4. Do not require a separate direct URL for FHIR capability statements if endpoints are collected.
5. Require issuers to provide a single URL for authorization/authentication protocols and implementation details.
6. Align endpoint reporting with the NDH IG Endpoint Profile resource.
7. If NDH IG alignment is finalized, provide 90 days after the final rule effective date for implementation.
8. Limit simultaneous mandatory IG version support by establishing retirement timelines or support caps.
9. Formalize public sandbox environments using synthetic datasets.
10. Evaluate testing tools using IG validation, sandbox compatibility, and public availability criteria.
11. Avoid rigid interoperability testing beyond initial conformance validation.
12. Publish standardized conformance test suites for issuer self-validation.
13. Explore incentives for interoperability across individual, Medicaid, large group, and Medicare markets.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Incomplete/inaccurate clinical data, manual provider workflows, reporting burden, multiple mandatory IG version burden, production instability, and cross-market data gaps.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Denials from missing information, patient confusion during issuer transitions, administrative costs, FWA risk, and incomplete medical history for ICHRA users.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Provider non-participation, fax/phone workflows, developer burden, upfront NDH alignment costs, testing/certification maturity, and issuer variation.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** 28%-35% of PA denials attributed to missing or inaccurate information; 59% of physicians completed PAs by phone and 45% used fax in a 2022 AMA survey; Oscar and other issuers committed to approving at least 80% of medical ePA requests in real time; 90-day transition period commitment for existing PAs.
- **Studies or research referenced:** CMS Health Technology Ecosystem overview; Muni Health 2026 guide; AMA 2022 prior-authorization fax survey; AHIP 2025 prior authorization commitments; Oscar Diabetes plan information.
- **Examples provided:** Incorrect patient information; incomplete clinical histories; payer transitions; ICHRA transition from large-group to individual-market plan.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Issuers, providers, patients, Medicare/Medicaid providers, third-party developers, CMS, ICHRA enrollees.
- **Economic implications:** Reduced administrative costs and FWA; upfront development costs for NDH IG alignment and sandbox/test infrastructure.
- **Technical feasibility:** Strongly technical comment; supports FHIR APIs, NDH IG alignment, synthetic-data sandboxes, standardized test suites, and lifecycle guardrails.
- **Patient care impact:** Improved continuity, fewer denials due to missing data, faster approvals, less confusion during payer transitions.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with modifications
- **Tone:** Technical, collaborative, implementation-focused
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Oscar welcomes the expansion of these rules to drugs." - Context: Overall support for the proposed rule.
2. "CMS should require providers that accept Medicare and Medicaid patients to submit requests electronically." - Context: Shared accountability recommendation.
3. "CMS should develop a centralized repository for issuers to report API endpoints for each required interoperability API." - Context: API endpoint reporting recommendation.
4. "CMS should formalize the use of public sandbox environments populated with synthetic datasets." - Context: Testing and certification recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Argues manual provider workflows undermine ePA and asks providers to submit electronically with complete data.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Detailed recommendations for API endpoints, NDH IG, sandboxes, and conformance testing.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Supports mandatory IGs but asks for lifecycle guardrails and limits on simultaneous versions.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports centralized endpoint reporting and implementation detail publication.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Emphasizes collaboration between issuers, providers, developers, and CMS.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Addresses developer burden, testing tools, and sandbox environments.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Seeks to replace fax/phone/manual workflows with electronic PA.
